name: Little Girl and Maximum Sum
description: The little girl loves the problems on array queries very much. One day she came across a rather well-known problem: you've got an array of $$$n$$$ elements (the elements of the array are indexed starting from 1); also, there are $$$q$$$ queries, each one is defined by a pair of integers $$$l_i$$$, $$$r_i$$$ $$$(1 \le l_i \le r_i \le n)$$$. You need to find for each query the sum of elements of the array with indexes from $$$l_i$$$ to $$$r_i$$$, inclusive. The little girl found the problem rather boring. She decided to reorder the array elements before replying to the queries in a way that makes the sum of query replies maximum possible. Your task is to find the value of this maximum sum.
input_specification: The first line contains two space-separated integers $$$n$$$ ($$$1 \le n \le 2\cdot10^5$$$) and $$$q$$$ ($$$1 \le q \le 2\cdot10^5$$$) — the number of elements in the array and the number of queries, correspondingly. The next line contains $$$n$$$ space-separated integers $$$a_i$$$ ($$$1 \le a_i \le 2\cdot10^5$$$) — the array elements. Each of the following $$$q$$$ lines contains two space-separated integers $$$l_i$$$ and $$$r_i$$$ ($$$1 \le l_i \le r_i \le n$$$) — the $$$i$$$-th query.
output_specification: In a single line print, a single integer — the maximum sum of query replies after the array elements are reordered. Please, do not use the %lld specifier to read or write 64-bit integers in C++. It is preferred to use the cin , cout streams or the %I64d specifier.
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 276C — Little Girl and Maximum Sum [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
